title: Pride And Prejudice: CHAPTER LV
enhanced_title: Chapter 55: The Courtship of Mr. Bingley and Jane Bennet
author: Jane Austen
description: Mr. Bingley renews his attentions to Jane Bennet, culminating in his proposal and their engagement, bringing joy to the Bennet family and marking a significant turning point in the novel.

analysis_entries.paragraph: This chapter marks the climax of the Bingley-Jane romance subplot, with Mr. Bingley's return to Longbourn signaling the resolution of months of suspense. Austen employs dramatic irony throughout—the reader, along with Elizabeth, understands that Darcy's intervention previously separated the couple, while Jane remains ignorant of this fact. The chapter demonstrates Austen's mastery of domestic comedy, nowhere more vividly than when Mrs. Bennet bursts in crying, 'Never mind Miss Lizzy's hair.'

Mrs. Bennet serves as the chapter's comic engine, her frantic attempts to leave Jane and Bingley alone providing both humor and social commentary on the marriage market. Her dramatic interruption of her daughters' dressing routine reveals the hierarchy of matrimonial priorities in the Bennet household. The mother's machinations, while embarrassing to Jane, are ultimately vindicated: 'in the evening Mrs. Bennet's invention was again at work to get everybody away from him and her daughter.'

The chapter explores the theme of feminine agency—or its limitations—through the contrast between Mrs. Bennet's active scheming and Jane's passive acceptance of her romantic fate. Jane's character remains consistent with her established disposition: modest, grateful, and assuming she is unworthy of such happiness. Her declaration ''Tis too much! by far too much. I do not deserve it' reinforces Austen's critique of the excessive modesty expected of women.

Mr. Bennet's blessing of the match provides both humor and genuine sentiment. His prediction that the couple will 'always exceed your income' due to their generous natures offers a wry assessment of their compatible temperaments. Unlike his usual sarcastic detachment, Mr. Bennet's happiness here is unmistakable: 'when Mr. Bennet joined them at supper, his voice and manner plainly showed how really happy he was.'

analysis_entries.paragraph: Elizabeth's role as observer and confidante positions her as the novel's moral center. Her satisfaction at the 'happiest, wisest, and most reasonable end' to Bingley's courtship reflects her growth in understanding—she now comprehends Darcy's earlier interference and its resolution. Her conversation with Bingley establishes their future brother-sister relationship, as he 'claimed the good wishes and affection of a sister.'
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
He then shut the door, and, coming up to her, claimed the good wishes
and affection of a sister.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Austen uses the chapter to contrast different models of happiness through the sisters' dialogue. Jane's wish that Elizabeth could be equally happy foreshadows the novel's resolution, while Elizabeth's self-aware declaration that she 'never could be so happy' without Jane's disposition reveals her continued struggle with her own character. The comic reference to 'another Mr. Collins' underscores the limited and precarious nature of women's marital prospects in this society.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: I may meet with another Mr. Collins in time.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The chapter concludes with a meditation on reputation and social perception. The Bennets' transformation from 'marked out for misfortune' to 'the luckiest family in the world' within weeks illustrates the volatility of community judgment. Mrs. Bennet's indiscreet whispering campaign, while comic, reinforces the novel's concern with how information circulates: 'she ventured, without any permission, to do the same by all her neighbours in Meryton.'

summary: Chapter 55 of Pride and Prejudice brings the Bingley-Jane romance to its joyful conclusion. Mr. Bingley's return to Longbourn, his strategically timed visits, and his eventual proposal represent the resolution of a subplot that has developed throughout the novel. The chapter excels in its comic portrayal of Mrs. Bennet's matchmaking schemes while delivering genuine emotional satisfaction through the engagement. Elizabeth's role as witness to her sister's happiness prepares the reader for her own romantic resolution, while the reactions of the Bennet family provide individual character moments—from Mr. Bennet's paternal blessing to Kitty's envious hopes. Austen uses this chapter to explore themes of social perception, feminine modesty, and the contrast between active scheming and passive acceptance in matters of marriage.
